The Seminole killifish Fundulus seminolis is a common species in freshwater systems of the southeastern United States, yet detailed life-history data remain sparse. Field collections indicate that individuals typically attain an ultimate standard length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm], a size that positions this species as one of the larger members of its genus. Achieving this maximum dimension requires sustained somatic growth over several growing seasons under favorable conditions. In concert with this length, the corresponding ultimate wet weight has been estimated from length-mass regressions at approximately 30.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 30.8 grams], a value that reflects the robust body condition of mature adults in productive lacustrine habitats. These asymptotic measures provide a benchmark for understanding the energetic demands placed on reproductively active individuals, particularly as they allocate resources toward gonad development. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been recorded at 5% [GSI = 5%] in individuals maintained at a stable laboratory temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C].

The onset of reproductive capability in Seminole killifish is marked by the attainment of a specific body size rather than a strict chronological age. Analysis of field-caught specimens reveals that the total length at puberty is approximately 6 cm [Lp = approximately 6 cm], a threshold that is typically reached within the first year of life in populations inhabiting warm, productive waters. Individuals below this size rarely exhibit gonadal development, suggesting that a critical somatic mass must be achieved before the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis is fully activated. This size-based maturation strategy is common among fundulids and likely reflects the necessity of accumulating sufficient energy reserves to support the physiological costs of gametogenesis and spawning behavior. Once this size is attained, fish transition from a strictly somatic growth trajectory to one that includes periodic reproductive episodes. The relationship between body size and maturity underscores the importance of environmental conditions that promote rapid early growth, as delayed maturation can reduce lifetime reproductive output and population resilience.

Reproductive output begins from a very small initial investment. Recently hatched prolarvae emerge from the chorion at a wet weight at birth of 0.0046 g [Wwb = 0.0046 g]rams, a diminutive size that is consistent with the small egg diameter documented in related fundulid species. This minimal starting mass places the newly emerged yolk-sac larva in a precarious energetic position, as it must rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition to first feeding occurs. The success of this early life stage is highly dependent on water temperature, as developmental rates and yolk absorption efficiency are tightly coupled to thermal conditions. The ability of these larvae to rapidly locate and capture suitable microplanktonic prey following the onset of exogenous feeding is critical for survival through the first days post-hatching. Mortality during this period is typically high, and only a fraction of the initial cohort survives to the juvenile stage under natural conditions, with predation and starvation acting as primary selective forces.

Maximum longevity in this species has been assessed through both field mark-recapture studies and controlled laboratory observations. Under typical environmental temperatures of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the time since birth at death can reach approximately 730 days [am = approximately 730 days]. This relatively short duration, equivalent to roughly two years, is characteristic of many small-bodied cyprinodontiform fishes that inhabit seasonally variable environments. Such a brief lifespan places considerable selective pressure on early reproduction to ensure population persistence. In the laboratory setting, maintaining a constant temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C] appears to support sustained physiological function without inducing the thermal stress that might accelerate senescence at higher temperatures, though it also does not provide the metabolic advantages of warmer conditions that could shorten lifespan through increased rates of cellular damage. Field records suggest that some individuals may survive into a third year, particularly in habitats with stable thermal regimes and reduced predation pressure, but the majority of the population is replaced annually.

Comparative analyses among fundulid species reveal that life-history variation correlates with habitat stability and latitude. For instance, the ultimate wet weight of 30.8 grams [Wwi = 30.8 grams] places Fundulus seminolis at an intermediate position among congeners—some smaller fundulids rarely exceed 15 grams, while others may surpass 50 grams under optimal conditions. Such variation reflects a generalist ecology that permits occupation of a range of freshwater environments. Likewise, the ultimate standard length of 16 cm [Li = 16 cm] represents a maximum body dimension only realized in highly productive lacustrine habitats. The gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] was recorded at 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This is reinforced by the modest size at puberty of 6 cm [Lp = 6 cm] total length and a maximum lifespan of 730 days [am = 730 days] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], which together position Fundulus seminolis as an opportunistic colonizer of dynamic freshwater ecosystems.
